portName: Port of Cádiz (Muelle Alfonso XIII and Muelle Ciudad)
seoTitle: Cádiz cruise port guide: walk to town, Seville by train
seoDescription: Cádiz cruise port 2026: ships dock 5 min from the old town. Cathedral €12, Torre Tavira €8, Roman Theatre free. Seville 1h25–1h50 by train each way.
quickAnswer: Ships dock at the Alfonso XIII and Ciudad quays, and the old town starts about 5 minutes' walk from the terminals; there is no tender. Everything in Cádiz is on foot on flat streets. For Seville, allow 1h25–1h50 each way by train from Cádiz station and be on a return train by 13:30 for a 17:30 all-aboard.
intro: Cádiz is one of the easiest cruise calls in Spain. The terminals sit against the old town, which fills a flat peninsula almost surrounded by sea, so you walk off the ship and into the streets in minutes. The cathedral, the Roman Theatre, Torre Tavira, the central market and La Caleta beach all fit into one unhurried day. The real decision is whether to leave town for Seville or Jerez. Both are on the railway from Cádiz station, a short walk from the quay, but Seville leaves only about three hours on the ground.

terminals.name: Alfonso XIII cruise terminal
terminals.notes: Main terminal, 1,300 m² after its expansion, with check-in desks, luggage storage, tourist information, free Wi-Fi and shops. The city's free Hospitality Desk for cruise passengers, staffed by multilingual tourist-information officers, hands out maps and opening hours. Taxi rank and coach parking outside.

terminals.name: Ciudad cruise terminal (Muelle Ciudad)
terminals.notes: Smaller second terminal of 420 m² with free Wi-Fi, opening onto Paseo de Canalejas and Plaza de San Juan de Dios.

terminals.name: Reina Victoria maritime station
terminals.notes: Not a cruise terminal: the passenger station for the metropolitan catamarans to El Puerto de Santa María and Rota.

walkability.detail: Flat and short. Plaza de San Juan de Dios is at the port exit, the cathedral and the Mercado Central are about 12 minutes on foot, and La Caleta is about 20 minutes across the peninsula. Castillo de Santa Catalina is a few minutes further along the shore. Pavements in the old town are narrow, and cars pass close in the smaller streets.

transportSections.detail: The best way to see Cádiz. Start at Plaza de San Juan de Dios, go through the Barrio del Pópulo to the cathedral and Roman Theatre, then west through the grid of streets to La Caleta.

transportSections.mode: City bus lines 1 and 7 to Playa de la Victoria
transportSections.cost: Pay on board or with a Consorcio card; check the fare at the stop
transportSections.detail: Line 1 runs from Plaza de España, near the port, along Avenida de Andalucía to Cortadura, from early morning until after midnight. Lines 1 and 7 both stop a short walk from Playa de la Victoria. Holders of a Consorcio de Transportes card pay €0.77 per urban trip in Cádiz (2026).

transportSections.mode: Train to Seville (Alvia or Media Distancia)
transportSections.cost: From about €10 one way when booked ahead; around €26 on average (2026)
transportSections.detail: About 15 trains a day from Cádiz station, a short walk south of the cruise quays, to Sevilla Santa Justa. Book a specific outbound and return train on renfe.com before the day; cruise days fill early trains.

transportSections.mode: Train to Jerez de la Frontera (Cercanías or Media Distancia)
transportSections.cost: Check Renfe; Cercanías is the cheapest option
transportSections.detail: More than 30 trains a day from Cádiz station, many via San Fernando and El Puerto de Santa María. Jerez is known for its sherry bodegas and the Royal Andalusian School of Equestrian Art; book either ahead.

transportSections.mode: Catamaran to El Puerto de Santa María or Rota
transportSections.cost: Check at the Reina Victoria station
transportSections.detail: Metropolitan catamarans leave from the Reina Victoria maritime station next to the cruise quays. A relaxed half-day alternative to the train.

transportSections.cost: Metered; ask for an estimate first
transportSections.detail: A rank stands outside the Alfonso XIII terminal on cruise days. Useful for Playa de la Victoria or a quick return from the far end of the old town.

returnTiming.rule: In Cádiz, start walking back 75 minutes before all-aboard (16:15 for a 17:30 all-aboard). From Seville, be on a train back no later than 13:30.
returnTiming.detail: From anywhere in the old town the walk back is 5–25 minutes. The Seville train takes up to 1h50, plus the walk from Cádiz station, and with a train return you should be on board 90 minutes before all-aboard. A 13:30 departure meets that with a little to spare; anything later does not.
returnTiming.emergencyFallback: If a train is cancelled or late, take the next one and call the port agent number in your daily programme at once. A taxi from Seville is about 120 km by road. Inside Cádiz, a taxi from the rank at Plaza de San Juan de Dios or a brisk walk gets you back in minutes.

diyVsExcursion.ship: Varies by line; check your cruise planner
diyVsExcursion.diy: €12 cathedral + €8 Torre Tavira; Roman Theatre and Santa Catalina free (2026)

diyVsExcursion.diy: Return train from about €20 booked ahead (2026), plus entries in Seville

excursionAdvice: Cádiz itself needs no excursion: it is flat, compact and next to the ship, and two of its main sights are free. Seville is where a ship tour earns its price. The train is 1h25–1h50 each way, so a 17:30 all-aboard leaves about three hours in the city, and a coach booked through the ship waits for you if traffic is bad. Go to Seville on your own only with booked trains and a firm 13:30 return. Jerez is the easier independent trip, with frequent trains of about 35–45 minutes.

dayPlan.intro: Assumes docking at 08:00 on a weekday and a day in Cádiz on foot.

steps.what: Walk off the ship to Plaza de San Juan de Dios, about 5 minutes.
Coffee, then through the Barrio del Pópulo, the oldest quarter.
Cathedral at opening (€12), then the Roman Theatre next door, which opens at 10:00 from October to March and 11:00 from April to September.
Mercado Central: the food stalls in the Rincón Gastronómico open around midday.
Torre Tavira (€8) for the camera obscura and rooftop view; book the slot online the day before.
Lunch in La Viña, the neighbourhood behind La Caleta.
La Caleta beach and Castillo de Santa Catalina (free).
Back along the sea wall and the Alameda to Plaza de España and the Monument to the Constitution of 1812.

sights.name: Cádiz Cathedral
sights.why: The large domed cathedral facing the sea, built over the 18th and 19th centuries, with the Torre del Reloj bell tower and the Casa de la Contaduría museum alongside.
sights.cost: €12; €11 over-65s; €10 students aged 13–25; under-12s free with an adult (2026)
sights.tip: Open Monday to Saturday 10:00–20:00 and Sunday 13:30–20:00, last entry 19:00. The Casa de la Contaduría closes at 16:30 and is shut on Sundays. Hours change at short notice for services.

sights.name: Torre Tavira
sights.why: An 18th-century watchtower once used to look out for merchant ships, with a camera obscura that projects live views of the city.
sights.tip: Visits run by booked slot; book online ahead. Open 10:00–18:00 from October to April and 10:00–20:00 from May to September, last entry an hour before closing.

sights.name: Roman Theatre (Teatro Romano)
sights.why: A Roman theatre uncovered beneath the houses of the Barrio del Pópulo, the oldest quarter.
sights.tip: Open Monday to Saturday 10:00–16:30 from October to March and 11:00–17:00 from April to September; Sunday 10:00–14:00. Closed on the first Monday of each month. Only 15 people at a time, so expect a short queue.

sights.name: Mercado Central
sights.why: The city's covered market since 1838, with fish counters and an outdoor wing of food stalls.
sights.tip: Closed on Sundays. Most food stalls open around 12:00–16:00, Tuesday to Saturday; see the fish counters before 13:00.

sights.name: La Caleta
sights.why: The old town's own beach, between two forts, with calmer water than the open Atlantic beaches.
sights.tip: About 20 minutes on foot from the port. Little shade; take water in summer.

sights.name: Castillo de Santa Catalina
sights.why: A star-shaped fort begun in 1598 after an English raid, now used for exhibitions.
sights.tip: Open daily, about 10:00–19:45, with shorter hours on event days. Look for the window in the wall that frames La Caleta.

sights.name: Oratorio de San Felipe Neri
sights.why: An oval Baroque church where the Cortes met to draft the Constitution of 1812, with an Immaculate Conception by Murillo.
sights.tip: In the old town between the market and the Alameda; a good stop on a wet day.

sights.name: Plaza de España and the Monument to the Constitution of 1812
sights.why: The large monument to Spain's first constitution, drafted in this city.
sights.tip: Close to the port gates; an easy last stop before reboarding.

beaches.name: La Caleta
beaches.howToGetThere: Walk west across the old town.
beaches.note: Sheltered between the castles of Santa Catalina and San Sebastián.

beaches.name: Playa de la Victoria
beaches.howToGetThere: City bus line 1 or 7 along Avenida de Andalucía, or Cercanías to Estadio or Segunda Aguada.
beaches.note: More than 3 km of sand on the Atlantic side of the modern city, with beach bars and a promenade.

commonMistakes.mistake: Going to Seville without a firm return plan.
commonMistakes.fix: Book both trains, and be on a return service by 13:30 for a 17:30 all-aboard; otherwise take the ship's tour.

commonMistakes.mistake: Paying for a taxi or tour bus to reach the old town.
commonMistakes.fix: The centre starts about 5 minutes' walk from the terminals.

commonMistakes.mistake: Turning up at Torre Tavira without a booking.
commonMistakes.fix: Visits run in timed slots; book online the day before.

commonMistakes.mistake: Planning the Roman Theatre for the afternoon or the first Monday of the month.
commonMistakes.fix: It closes at 16:30 in winter, 17:00 in summer and 14:00 on Sundays, and shuts on the first Monday. Go in the morning.

commonMistakes.mistake: Saving the market for a Sunday call.
commonMistakes.fix: The Mercado Central is closed on Sundays. Eat in La Viña instead.

safety: Cádiz is a relaxed city for daytime visitors. Take normal care with bags and phones in crowded spots: the Mercado Central, Plaza de San Juan de Dios and busy trains to Seville. Do not leave valuables on the sand at La Caleta. Summer sun is strong and shade is scarce on the beaches; carry water. Some old-town streets are narrow, with cars passing close to the pavement.
scams: Pickpockets in crowds at the Mercado Central and on trains to Seville. Keep bags zipped and in front.
Card machines offering to charge you in your home currency (dynamic currency conversion). Always choose to pay in euros.
In Seville, women offering sprigs of rosemary near the cathedral and then demanding money for a fortune. Do not accept anything handed to you.
accessibility: Cádiz suits limited mobility better than most Spanish ports: the terminals open straight onto the old town and the peninsula is flat. Pavements are narrow and some are uneven, and cars pass close in small streets. Torre Tavira involves stairs. The Roman Theatre limits numbers to 15 at a time; ask staff about access. Trains to Seville are the more demanding option; a ship's coach tour may be easier.
rainyDay: Stay in the old town: the cathedral, Oratorio de San Felipe Neri, the Mercado Central and Torre Tavira are all indoors and within 15 minutes of the ship, though the camera obscura works best in clear weather. A train to Jerez with a booked bodega tour also suits a wet day.
crowdTips: Cádiz handled 255,170 cruise passengers on 158 calls in the first half of 2026, up 21% on 2025. Spring and autumn are the peaks; the port lists 43 calls for October 2026 alone, and days with three or four ships happen. When several ships are in, the cathedral, the Mercado Central and Plaza de San Juan de Dios are busiest from about 10:00 to 13:00. Do the cathedral at opening and save La Caleta and Santa Catalina for the early afternoon. No tourist tax was in force in Andalusia when checked in October 2026.

faqs.q: Is Cádiz cruise port walkable to the old town?
faqs.a: Yes. The Alfonso XIII and Ciudad terminals are on the edge of the old town, about 5 minutes from Plaza de San Juan de Dios. The cathedral is about 12 minutes on foot and La Caleta about 20.
No. Ships dock at the city quays, usually Alfonso XIII or Ciudad.

faqs.q: How do I get from Cádiz cruise port to Seville?
faqs.a: Walk to Cádiz station and take an Alvia (about 1h25) or Media Distancia train (about 1h50) to Sevilla Santa Justa. Fares start at about €10 one way when booked ahead (2026). Be on a return train by 13:30 for a 17:30 all-aboard.

faqs.q: How do I get from Cádiz cruise port to Jerez?
faqs.a: Take a Cercanías or Media Distancia train from Cádiz station; the trip takes 32–45 minutes and trains are frequent.
€12 general, €11 for over-65s and €10 for students aged 13–25; under-12s with an adult go free (2026). Open Monday to Saturday 10:00–20:00 and Sunday from 13:30.

faqs.q: What can I do in Cádiz in one day from a cruise ship?
faqs.a: Walk the old town: the cathedral, the Roman Theatre, the Mercado Central and Torre Tavira, then lunch in La Viña and an hour at La Caleta and Castillo de Santa Catalina.
La Caleta is about 20 minutes' walk. Playa de la Victoria, the long Atlantic beach, is about 15 minutes on city bus line 1 or 7.

faqs.q: Is Cádiz safe for cruise passengers?
faqs.a: Yes. Take normal care with bags in the market, in busy squares and on trains.
